source.title: Baseline Shape Decides the Verdict: A Controlled Re-Examination of Ternary Language Models at 60K Parameters

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether architecture shape matters little at a fixed parameter count and reports large loss differences across shapes at 16M bytes, qualifying the claim. It does not fit scaling laws or test compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study tests V4 with parameter-matched model and shape comparisons using held-out validation loss. Its discussion of scaling-law papers and its audit of the earlier Atome-LM comparisons are not new tests of V1–V3 or V7; those versions are not tested here.
record.test_reason: The study trains five parameter-matched transformer shapes (1×52 to 6×24, within 3% of 60.8K parameters) and compares held-out validation loss. That bears directly on V4 in a new setting: byte-level models of about 60K parameters on TinyStories V2, two short budgets, FP32 and ternary. The paper is about ternary architecture comparisons, not scaling laws, and offers no argument against V4, so T3 fits better than the reader's T5. It fits no scaling curves, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude four things at 60K parameters. First, the routed model's short-budget advantage is at least partly a baseline-shape artifact, and the best transformer shape changes with budget. Second, the routed model's gain at 130M bytes does not require routing, since a plain gated SSM does at least as well. Third, the ternary penalty differs by architecture, but three alternative explanations remain. Fourth, a 90/10 full-precision-then-ternary schedule wins only with a stage-2 learning rate about 10× the pretraining peak. They state that nothing is established beyond 60K parameters or TinyStories.
record.recipe_differences: This is a controlled small-model architecture and shape study, not a test that fits the original scaling laws; it uses 60K-parameter byte-level models, TinyStories V2, two training-byte budgets, and held-out loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Shape ordering changes with budget: the shallow-wide transformer is best at 16M bytes and worst among the tested transformer shapes at 130M bytes. The shapes also vary in depth, width, FFN ratio, and positional-embedding share.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched parameter count (about 60K) and 130M bytes, the routed hybrid beats each tested transformer shape by 22.2–24.0% FP32. The gated SSM beats the routed model by a further 9.1%. At 16M bytes the architecture gaps are inside noise against the best transformer shape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture family (recurrent vs transformer) changes loss substantially at fixed small parameter count, depending on training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Ternary penalty at 130M differs by architecture: +5.3% best transformer, +19.5% routed, +28.1% gated SSM. It is confounded by unequal quantization and an untuned learning rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-bit precision cost depends on architecture and training budget at tiny scale.

record.problems: All experiments use one parameter count and one byte-level corpus. Only three transformer shapes were evaluated at 130M bytes. Shape comparisons vary depth, width, FFN ratio, and positional-embedding share together; the authors caution that the shallow-wide shape is not a pure depth/width comparison. The gated SSM has 5.6% more parameters than the routed model. Results do not establish behavior at other sizes or corpora.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant measured shape or architecture comparison was left out. The audited Atome-LM results in §4 are prior-work results, not runs performed in this study, so they are not recorded as rows.

untested.parts: Only one parameter count (about 60K) and one byte-level corpus. The two deepest shapes were not run at 130M bytes. Shapes were matched on total rather than non-embedding parameters. Learning rate was not tuned per shape. No converged or long-budget runs.
No sweep over parameters, data or compute.
No power-law fits in other regimes; ternary runs at two budgets only.
No downstream tasks; loss is the only metric.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's third label (architecture families challenge V4) is dropped: cross-family differences are not what V4 claims, and Kaplan et al. themselves report transformer vs LSTM differences. Several issues weaken the 16M result as a test of V4. Kaplan matches non-embedding parameters, but here learned positional embeddings take 11–22% of transformer parameters, so non-embedding counts differ across shapes. The 6×24 shape has aspect ratio 4, likely outside the 'wide range' in Kaplan et al. The 16M budget is only 245 steps. The authors say shape means 'the whole depth/width/FFN/position-budget package'. The four extra shapes beyond the pre-specified 3×32 were added post hoc.

versions.untested_parts: No loss sweep over parameter count, training tokens, or compute to test power-law scaling.
No fits on smaller runs or predictions for much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search over parameter and token allocations.

Tests several shapes at 60K parameters on TinyStories V2 at two byte budgets; only three transformer shapes were evaluated at 130M bytes. Does not establish how shape effects behave at other parameter counts, corpora, or tokenizations.
No other modalities or training regimes are evaluated.
No scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared.

rows.operation_detail: Measured held-out validation loss in the transformer shape sweep.
rows.measure: Validation loss (nats/byte), mean over three seeds
rows.note: Best full-precision transformer shape at this budget; transformer shapes span 2.835–3.477 nats/byte.
rows.check: These rows are one shape sweep, not separate observations. The 'slight effect' V4 predicts is absent: FP32 loss spans 2.835–3.477, a 22.6% spread. Shapes also differ in FFN ratio (2d vs 4d) and positional-embedding share (11–22%). Matching is on total parameters, not non-embedding parameters as in Kaplan. Budget is only 245 optimizer steps.

relationships.condition: Five parameter-matched transformer shapes at 16M bytes (245 steps), FP32 and ternary
relationships.reason: Loss spans 22.6% FP32 (r1–r5) and about 21% ternary (r6–r10), so shape matters a lot at this short budget. The study links this to budget (ordering reverses at 130M), and confounds remain: FFN ratio, positional-embedding share, matching on total parameters.
relationships.display_finding: Loss varied by 22.6% for FP32 and about 21% for ternary models at the short budget, with rankings reversing at 130M bytes, while FFN ratio and positional-embedding share also varied.

relation.reason: The study measures held-out loss across approximately parameter-matched transformer shapes, directly testing V4.

tranche.reason: The short-budget shape sweep directly shows that V4 needs restating: parameter-matched shapes produce large loss differences, while longer-budget differences are small.

source_check.notes: Budget changes data seen, optimizer steps and schedule length together; the two deepest shapes were not evaluated at 130M bytes. Table 4 shows FP32 ranking reverses with budget, but ternary ranking does not, despite Figure 1's caption.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The recurrent models have substantially lower losses than the transformer shapes in the reported comparisons, showing that architectural differences can matter more than slightly (rows r11–r16, r21–r24).
